articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'EMC and the Motor Vehicle' (Digest No.055)
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on EMC and the Motor Vehicle (Digest No: 1992/055)
1992 IEE Colloquium on EMC and the Motor Vehicle (Digest No: 1992/055)
abstract: Automotive electrical components, such as motors and microprocessor based circuitry, cause voltage and current disturbances in their power supplies when operated. These disturbances generate electromagnetic interference (EMI) which is radiated from the harness. The interference may occur across a range of frequencies and can disturb communications in the locality of the vehicle. If the interference is of a significant level at frequencies within the radio broadcast bands then it is called radio frequency interference (RFI). The techniques used to measure RFI cannot encompass every aspect of the interference signal's frequency and time varying characteristics. Techniques which are most representative of the subjective effects for particular conditions of interference signal characteristics and receiver design are discussed. These include open area testing, individual component testing, measurements at the aerial connector, and SINAD based measurements. A strategy to deal with RFI performance is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on EMC and the Motor Vehicle (Digest No: 1992/055)
abstract: The author describes some preliminary work being carried out on the numerical prediction of currents flowing on cables in cars, when the care is illuminated by external electromagnetic radiation. A computational design tool would allow a number of alternative cable installations to be rapidly examined for susceptibility, and the optimum parameters selected. The author describes an approach to computing the currents on cables. The electromagnetic model which is used to predict the fields in the neighbourhood and the interior of the car due to an incident wave is described. Some colour graphics produced using this type of model and showing the amplitudes of field components are presented. Methods of calculating currents on cables using the predicted fields are described. Some preliminary results showing predicted field components along a cable, and the current flowing, are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Some impedance measurements on a low frequency EMC illumination antenna
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on EMC and the Motor Vehicle (Digest No: 1992/055)
abstract: The EMC chamber at Rover Group's Gaydon Test Centre is used to perform a wide range of RF emission and susceptibility tests over a very wide range of frequencies. The author reports briefly on some impedance measurements performed on a purpose-built 'parallel line' antenna used in that chamber for vehicle susceptibility tests in the frequency range 3 MHz-50 MHz. The impedance measurements were performed for: the impedance presented by the antenna alone; the impedance characteristic with a Mini placed under the antenna; the impedance characteristic with a fastback under the antenna; and the impedance characteristic with a Discovery under the antenna.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A study of aspects of EMC performance of vehicles fitted with transceiver systems
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on EMC and the Motor Vehicle (Digest No: 1992/055)
abstract: The author describes a series of measurements made and the results obtained during a study of the EMC performance of a vehicle fitted with radio equipment. The subject vehicle was a government service vehicle and consequently also had additional equipment fitted which may have compromised the EMC performance of the vehicle. The tests performed were: SINAD tests, susceptibility tests, bulk current absorption; and bulk current injection testing. The results of the tests are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The bulk current absorption technique for evaluation of coupling between radiated fields and wiring harnesses
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on EMC and the Motor Vehicle (Digest No: 1992/055)
abstract: The wide range of EMC facilities and services at MIRA (Motor Industry Research Association) provide the ideal environment for evaluation and comparison of measurement techniques. Whole vehicle radiated immunity is most often used to assess the performance of vehicles and their subsystems when subjected to electromagnetic interference, whilst bench methods such as bulk current injection (BCI) are popular for development work on the subsystem alone. Work performed at MIRA suggests that the coupling between radiated fields and wiring harnesses is influenced by both the antenna position and the structure of the vehicle. Data obtained using the bulk current absorption (BCA) technique, where a current probe is used to measure the RF currents induced on the harness of the vehicle, is presented to demonstrate these effects and to suggest more suitable levels for the transfer function.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: EMC and the motor car-the Police Service experience
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on EMC and the Motor Vehicle (Digest No: 1992/055)
abstract: The author describes some of the problems encountered with Police Service Vehicles relating to interference in the electronic systems. The author describes problems in the engine management system and direction indicator flashers of the BMW K100 motorcycle caused by the on-board radio transmissions. Other problems with Jaguar and Rover 800 cars are also described. The solutions to all the problems are discussed. The measures taken to ensure EMC of Police vehicles are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The EMC Directive and the motor vehicle-a brief update
publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on EMC and the Motor Vehicle (Digest No: 1992/055)
abstract: The author discusses the latest situation regarding the EC EMC Directive and the automotive industry. The extension to the Directive and the subsequent proposals by the Association of European Automobile Construction (ACEA) are discussed. In particular the author mentions radiated emissions, radiated immunity, conducted transient emissions and immunity, and electrostatic discharge. The legislative situation relating the Directive are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: 1992 IEE Colloquium on EMC and the Motor Vehicle (Digest No: 1992/055)
abstract: The author describes the lessons learnt in operating Europe's first commissioned automotive electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) test facility and its development to provide cost effective, yet state of the art, whole vehicle susceptibility testing for Rover Cars. The Rover Group's Gaydon Test Centre was commissioned in March 1986. The facility is run on two shifts and is usually booked upto a year in advance. The internal walls and ceiling are lined with 1.2 m long radio absorbent material (RAM), carbon loaded foam pyramids, to reduce resonances and reflections and so permit controlled testing, in effect simulating open side conditions. The author discusses the costs involved in vehicle testing and how the costs can be reduced. The author covers body shapes, trim levels, aerials, the test state and alternative development testing. The efficiency of the test centre is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
